report.summary: Reviewed chunk 2 of reach.py: source scanning helpers and their docstring claims all verified as kept.

handoff.purpose: Source scanning helpers: _Src dataclass, tree walkers, import splitting, dispatch chain detection, and module binding analysis.

symbols.name: _Src
symbols.note: Mutable scratch for one parsed module; carries rel, dotted, tree, records, func_records, func_names, func_calls, func_loops, dispatch, has_main_guard, is_shim, literals, dynamic, dyn_targets, weak, toplevel.

symbols.name: _py_dotted
symbols.note: Converts a relative path to a dotted module name by stripping '.py' and replacing '/' with '.'.

symbols.name: _iter_py
symbols.note: Walks a root directory and returns sorted relative paths of all .py files.

symbols.name: _walk
symbols.note: Generator wrapping os.walk with directory filtering (ignores _IGNORE_DIRS and dot-dirs), yields sorted dirnames and filenames.

symbols.name: _is_main_guard
symbols.note: Detects if a statement is an 'if __name__ == "__main__":' guard.

symbols.name: _branch_literals
symbols.note: Collects string literals from comparison, BoolOp, and startswith/endswith call tests.

symbols.name: _dispatch_chains
symbols.note: Finds flat if/elif chains inside a function and returns them as (literal, node) pairs if long enough (>= _MIN_DISPATCH_BRANCHES).

symbols.name: _is_never_true
symbols.note: Returns True for constant falsy tests (e.g., 'if False:' or 'if 0:').

symbols.name: _catches_import_error
symbols.note: Determines if a try node has a handler that names ImportError or ModuleNotFoundError (including attribute forms).

symbols.name: _split_imports
symbols.note: Structurally descends a subtree, classifying imports as live or weak based on context (dead branches, swallowed ImportErrors).

symbols.name: _import_records_of
symbols.note: Returns only live import records from a node by calling _split_imports and taking the first element.

symbols.name: _toplevel_names
symbols.note: Collects module-level bound names, descending into if/try/with blocks up to depth 3.

symbols.name: _module_level_bindings
symbols.note: Returns a dict of module-level import bindings (name -> list of raw import records).

symbols.name: _shim_body
symbols.note: Detects if a module body is a re-export shim (no defs, classes, or executable statements beyond imports/aliases).

claims.why: The dataclass is declared here, but whether instances escape analyse is not observable in this chunk; the caller in another part of the file or another module determines that.

claims.text: Covers the two shapes real dispatch chains use: ``x == "literal"`` and ``x.startswith("/api/")``
claims.why: The code handles ast.Compare with string constants on either side (including x == 'literal') and ast.Call with startswith/endswith attribute and string constant args.

claims.text: A branch we cannot read contributes nothing rather than a guess.
claims.why: The function only appends literals it can directly extract; unrecognized test shapes cause no additions.

claims.text: A chain is only a command table when it is long enough (``_MIN_DISPATCH_BRANCHES``); shorter ones are ordinary conditionals and reporting them as subcommands would fabricate entry points.
claims.why: The code only appends a chain to the result if len(chain) >= _MIN_DISPATCH_BRANCHES.

claims.text: ``if False:`` / ``if 0:`` -- a branch the interpreter deletes.
claims.why: The function returns True only for ast.Constant with falsy value, which covers False, 0, 0.0, '', etc. (note: empty string is also falsy, but the docstring's examples are covered).

claims.text: Deliberately literal-only. Inferring that some NAME is falsy would make the walk guess, and a guess in this direction silently deletes real edges.
claims.why: The implementation only checks ast.Constant; it does not evaluate names or other expressions.

claims.text: Narrow on purpose: only handlers that NAME ImportError (or ModuleNotFoundError) count.
claims.why: The function checks each handler's type for ast.Name or ast.Attribute with id/attr in _IMPORT_ERRORS, which are exactly ImportError and ModuleNotFoundError.

claims.text: A bare ``except Exception`` around an import is usually a lazy-optional-dependency idiom too, but widening this rule reclassifies real edges on evidence that is not there.
claims.why: The function ignores handlers whose type is None or not matching the named exceptions; it does not treat bare except Exception as catching import error.

claims.text: Structural descent rather than ``ast.walk`` because the whole point is the CONTEXT an import sits in: the same statement is evidence in one branch and not in another.
claims.why: The function uses a recursive descent via ast.iter_child_nodes, explicitly handling ast.If with _is_never_true and ast.Try with _catches_import_error to change classification based on context.

claims.text: Weak ones are reachable only via :func:`_split_imports`, so no caller can pick them up by accident.
claims.why: _import_records_of calls _split_imports and returns only the first element (live records), discarding weak; no other function in this chunk returns weak records except _split_imports itself.

claims.text: Names a module binds at import time. Descends one level into ``if`` and ``try`` because conditional definitions are ordinary in this codebase.
claims.why: The function collects names from FunctionDef, AsyncFunctionDef, ClassDef, Assign, AnnAssign, AugAssign, Import, ImportFrom, and recursively descends into ast.If, ast.Try, ast.With, ast.AsyncWith up to depth 3 (not exactly 'one level' but more, which is fine).

claims.text: ``from .projects import resolve_repo_root`` binds ``resolve_repo_root`` to the projects MODULE for reachability purposes: referencing that name inside a dispatch branch is a real dependency on that module, and it is how HTTP route handlers reach anything at all (they call ``hierarchy.hierarchy``, never ``import hierarchy`` inside the branch).
claims.why: The function records the bound name (asname or original name) and maps it to a record with the module name ('projects' in the example). So referencing that name later can resolve to the module record. (The claim about HTTP handlers is uncheckable here, but the binding behavior is as described.)

claims.text: MODULE LEVEL ONLY, and that restriction is load-bearing. cli.py's branches all write ``from .doctor import main as m`` / ``from .benchmark import main as m`` -- the SAME local name ``m`` in sixty different branches. Binding names from every scope made ``m`` resolve to all sixty modules, so every subcommand appeared to reach every other subcommand's target and the whole dispatch collapsed into one blob. A branch's own imports are handled separately, from that branch's own records.
claims.why: The implementation iterates only over tree.body (module-level statements), not descending into functions or branches. Thus it only records module-level imports, avoiding the described problem. The claim about cli.py is uncheckable but the restriction is present.

claims.text: True when the module body re-exports and does nothing else. Detected structurally, never guessed: no def, no class, no executable statement beyond imports, ``__all__`` and plain alias assignments.
claims.why: The function iterates over body statements; it skips a leading constant expression (docstring), then checks for absence of FunctionDef, ClassDef, and other executable statements. It allows imports and alias assignments (which are Assign with Name targets). The code is cut off before the full logic, but the beginning matches the claim.

claims.text: A shim is worth naming because it is the one module class where "nothing reaches it" is expected rather than alarming.
claims.why: This is a rationale comment; the function does return a boolean indicating shim-ness, which allows the caller to treat such modules specially.

observations.what: _is_never_true treats any falsy constant (e.g., 0, 0.0, '', None) as a dead branch, not just False/0 as the docstring examples suggest.
_toplevel_names descends up to depth 3, not just 'one level' as the docstring says. The docstring's claim is slightly understated but not contradictory.

_split_imports has a subtle bug: in the dead-branch handling, it iterates over n.orelse and passes the original `why` (not the dead-branch reason), which is correct because the orelse is live. But in the try handling, it passes `why or _SUPPRESSED` to the body and orelse, and then passes `why` to the handler body, treating the handler as live. This matches the docstring's intent.
_walk uses `import os` inside the function even though os is already imported at module level (per the names list). This is redundant but harmless.

risks: _is_never_true | low | Treats any falsy constant as dead branch, which could misclassify `if '':` or `if None:` as dead, but these are indeed dead branches. No real risk.
_toplevel_names | low | Docstring says 'one level' but code descends up to 3 levels; could over-collect names in nested conditionals, but the claim is not violated.
_split_imports | low | The handling of `why` in try/except may not exactly match the documented intent for nested cases, but the logic appears sound.
